newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AMP board to meet this week amid float talk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AMP board to meet this week amid float talk.

text.p: The board of the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP), Australia's largest insurer and investment group with A$90 billion of funds under management, will meet next Wednesday but a spokesman would not say if the demutalisation of the life office was on the agenda.

The spokesman told Reuters that a taskforce, consisting of AMP executives and external advisers, was working on structural options but could not say if its report was finished and the recommendations ready for directors of the life office.

A member of AMP's New Zealand board, Rosanne Meo, was quoted in the New Zealand media late last week as saying AMP policyholders should know before Christmas whether AMP was going to follow other large Australasian life offices and demutualise.
Meo, who will become chairwoman of the New Zealand operations next month, was not available for comment.

Two AMP New Zealand officials referred all queries to AMP's corporate affairs chief manager James Willoughby in the Sydney head office but they said, however, that there was nothing wrong with the New Zealand reports.
AMP has been tight-lipped about its plans to possibly change its corporate structure and has repeatedly refused to say when the issue would be considered by its board.

It announced the review, including the demutualisation option, on January 18 this year and said then that due to the complex issues facing the taskforce it would not be in a position to comment further until the 1996 fourth quarter.
AMP managing director and chief executive George Trumbull is overseeing the work of the taskforce.

Trumbull said in May this year that a demutualisation -- where AMP's ownership shifts from private policyholders to a shareholder basis -- was not a sure thing and would be 10 times more complex than that faced by National Mutual Holdings Ltd or the upcoming structural change by Colonial Mutual.
Insurance sector analysts have told Reuters recently that it would be logical for AMP to demutualise and eventually list on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX).
They expect policyholders to become shareholders in a straight swap and perhaps have the option of taking a cash payout.
"In theory you could have a very big private company or a public company that is unlisted," one Sydney-based analyst said.
"But it would be very improbable. I think it would defeat one of the objectives which is to have access to capital markets so you would almost certainly want to float," he said.
An official with one of Australia's regulatory bodies said he believed AMP had held informal talks with the ASX but no commitments had been made.
"I think it (the likely float) is one of the worst kept secrets around town," the regulator said.
AMP would have the largest register of any Australian company if it listed and sit comfortably in the Top 20 companies and probably within the Top 10, brokers said.
National Mutual, which is 51 percent-owned by French insurance giant AXA SA, listed on October 8 and now ranks as Australia's 25th largest company with a market capitalisation of A$3.03 billion.
